pathophysiology.summary: Anaphylaxis is a serious systemic hypersensitivity reaction that is usually rapid in onset and may cause death (WAO 2020). Mast-cell and basophil mediators cause vasodilatation, capillary leak, bronchospasm and upper-airway oedema. Common triggers in India are drugs (antibiotics, NSAIDs, contrast), insect stings and foods. Intramuscular adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh is the first and most important treatment; there is no absolute contraindication to it (WAO 2020). Antihistamines and corticosteroids do not treat airway, breathing or circulation problems and must never delay adrenaline (RCUK 2021).
keyMechanisms: IgE-mediated or direct mast-cell activation releases histamine, tryptase and leukotrienes.
Vasodilatation and capillary leak cause distributive shock.
Bronchial smooth-muscle contraction and laryngeal oedema obstruct the airway.
Adrenaline reverses these through alpha and beta receptors.

pathophysiology.summary: Paracetamol is safe at therapeutic doses (up to 60 mg/kg/day, maximum 4 g/day in adults) but overdose saturates normal conjugation, so more drug is converted to the toxic metabolite NAPQI. When hepatic glutathione is used up, NAPQI causes centrilobular liver necrosis, which may progress to acute liver failure, kidney injury and death. Early patients often have no symptoms. Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is almost fully protective when started within 8 hours of ingestion; it still helps when started late or after liver injury (MJA 2020). Risk is judged from the dose ingested, the paracetamol concentration on the nomogram for single immediate-release ingestions, and ALT.
keyMechanisms: Overdose saturates glucuronidation and sulfation, so more paracetamol becomes NAPQI.
NAPQI binds liver proteins once glutathione is exhausted, causing centrilobular necrosis.
Acetylcysteine restores glutathione and detoxifies NAPQI.
Liver failure leads to coagulopathy, hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy and kidney injury.

clinicalManagement.title: Start acetylcysteine
actions: Immediate-release: treat if level on or above the nomogram line; start at once if a level cannot be obtained within 8 hours (MJA Box 3).

clinicalManagement.title: Stop or continue

If continuing: review and test at least every 12 hours.

Do not give clotting factors unless bleeding (MJA 2020).

pathophysiology.summary: Severe malaria is a medical emergency, usually from Plasmodium falciparum, though P. vivax can also cause severe disease in India. Parasitised red cells stick to small-vessel endothelium, blocking flow in the brain, kidneys and gut, while haemolysis and inflammation cause anaemia, acidosis and organ failure. Death can follow within hours. Parenteral artesunate is the treatment of choice; after at least 24 hours of parenteral treatment and once the patient can swallow, a full 3-day area-specific ACT is given (National Drug Policy 2013). Children under 6 years who cannot reach injectable treatment within 6 hours can be given rectal artesunate before referral (WHO 2017).
keyMechanisms: Parasitised red cells adhere to microvascular endothelium (sequestration).
Microvascular obstruction causes cerebral malaria, acute kidney injury (AKI) and lactic acidosis.
Haemolysis and splenic clearance cause severe anaemia and jaundice.
Parasite glucose consumption, quinine-induced insulin release and liver failure cause hypoglycaemia.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas caused mainly by gallstones and alcohol in India; others include hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalcaemia, drugs, trauma and post-ERCP. Premature activation of trypsin inside acinar cells digests the gland and triggers a systemic inflammatory response that can cause capillary leak, hypovolaemia and organ failure. Most attacks are mild and settle in days; severe disease with persistent organ failure (over 48 hours) carries high mortality (ACG 2024). Early care is fluid resuscitation with careful reassessment, pain control, early feeding, and treating the cause; antibiotics are only for infection (ACG 2024; NTG 2025).
keyMechanisms: Duct obstruction or alcohol triggers premature trypsinogen activation in acinar cells.
Autodigestion and cytokine release cause local necrosis and systemic inflammation.
Capillary leak causes hypovolaemia, haemoconcentration and organ failure.
Necrotic tissue can become infected, usually after the first week.

pathophysiology.summary: Hepatic encephalopathy is brain dysfunction caused by liver insufficiency or portosystemic shunting, ranging from subtle cognitive changes (covert HE) to coma. Gut-derived ammonia and other toxins bypass the failing liver, causing astrocyte swelling and altered neurotransmission. Most episodes in cirrhosis are triggered by a precipitant: infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, diuretic overuse, electrolyte disorders or constipation (AASLD/EASL Table 3); correcting it resolves most episodes. Lactulose is the first-line treatment; rifaximin is added to prevent recurrence. Blood ammonia does not diagnose, grade or predict HE (AASLD/EASL recommendation 9).
keyMechanisms: Failing liver and portosystemic shunts let gut-derived ammonia reach the brain.
Astrocytes convert ammonia to glutamine, causing swelling and low-grade cerebral oedema.
Inflammation from infection amplifies ammonia neurotoxicity.
Lactulose acidifies the colon and traps ammonia; rifaximin reduces ammonia-producing bacteria.

pathophysiology.summary: Hyperkalaemia is serum potassium of 5.5 mmol/L or more; 6.5 mmol/L or more is severe (UKKA). It lowers the resting membrane potential of cardiac cells, slowing conduction and risking bradycardia, ventricular fibrillation or asystole. Common causes in India are acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease, RAAS inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics, diabetic ketoacidosis and tissue breakdown. Treatment follows a fixed order: protect the heart with IV calcium if the ECG shows changes, shift potassium into cells with insulin-glucose and salbutamol, remove potassium with binders or dialysis, and monitor potassium and glucose closely (UKKA; ICMR STW).
keyMechanisms: Raised extracellular potassium partly depolarises myocytes, inactivating sodium channels and slowing conduction.
Calcium restores the threshold potential without lowering potassium.
Insulin and beta-2 agonists drive potassium into cells via Na+/K+-ATPase.
Binders and dialysis are the only treatments that remove potassium from the body.

pathophysiology.summary: Scabies is infestation of the skin by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, spread by close skin contact, often within families, hostels, schools and orphanages. The female mite burrows in the stratum corneum and lays eggs; itch comes from a hypersensitivity reaction to mites, eggs and faeces, so it starts 3–6 weeks after the first infestation but within 2–3 days on reinfestation (ICMR STW). Crusted scabies in immunosuppressed, neurologically impaired or disabled people carries huge mite numbers and is highly contagious. All household contacts must be treated at the same time, or reinfestation follows.
keyMechanisms: Female mites burrow into the stratum corneum and lay eggs.
Delayed hypersensitivity to mite products causes intense nocturnal itch and papules.
Scratching breaks the skin and allows staphylococcal and streptococcal infection.
Impaired immunity or inability to scratch allows mite numbers to rise into crusted scabies.

India has seen a rise in extensive, chronic and recurrent tinea, driven by heat and humidity, tight synthetic clothing, shared towels, and misuse of over-the-counter steroid-antifungal combination creams that suppress inflammation while letting fungus spread. Steroid use changes the appearance: rings may be incomplete, scaling minimal and pigmentation prominent (ICMR STW). Limited disease is treated with topical azoles or terbinafine; extensive or nail disease needs oral therapy until complete clearance, often 3–8 weeks or longer.

pathophysiology.summary: Stones in the common bile duct usually pass from the gallbladder and may block bile flow, causing obstructive jaundice. Bacteria then multiply in the stagnant, pressurised bile and enter the blood: acute cholangitis, with pain, fever with chills and jaundice, and in severe cases shock and confusion. Stones can also impact at the ampulla and trigger biliary pancreatitis. Diagnosis rests on deranged liver tests and a dilated duct on ultrasound, confirmed by MRCP or EUS. Treatment is resuscitation, antibiotics and, above all, biliary drainage, usually by ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone clearance, then cholecystectomy (ICMR STW; NTG 2025).
keyMechanisms: Gallstones migrate into the CBD and obstruct bile flow.
Raised biliary pressure drives bacteria and toxins into the blood (cholangiovenous reflux).
Ampullary impaction obstructs the pancreatic duct and causes pancreatitis.
Prolonged obstruction causes cholestatic liver injury and coagulopathy.

evidenceAudit.scope: Ascites in adults with cirrhosis in India: diagnostic paracentesis, salt restriction, diuretics, large-volume paracentesis with albumin, refractory ascites, and diagnosis, treatment and prophylaxis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), using the BSG/BASL ascites guideline (2020), the ICMR Acute Liver Failure / ACLF STW (2020) and NCDC-ICMR NTG 2025.
findings: Diagnostic paracentesis indications, SAAG 11 g/L or more for portal hypertension, SBP as ascitic neutrophils above 250/mm³, albumin 1.5 g/kg then 1 g/kg on day 3, salt 5–6.5 g/day, spironolactone 100–400 mg, furosemide 40–160 mg, weight-loss limits, albumin 8 g per litre for paracentesis over 5 L, secondary SBP prophylaxis doses and TIPSS cautions checked against BSG/BASL 2020.

Norfloxacin availability varies in India; ciprofloxacin or co-trimoxazole are alternatives.
Avoidance of NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors is standard practice, not confirmed in the opened extract.

pathophysiology.summary: Ascites is the commonest complication of cirrhosis and marks decompensation. Portal hypertension and splanchnic vasodilatation reduce effective arterial volume, activating renin-angiotensin-aldosterone and sympathetic systems, so the kidneys retain sodium and water that leak into the peritoneum. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is infection of ascitic fluid without a surgical source, often with few symptoms, and can trigger kidney failure and encephalopathy. Every patient admitted with ascites needs a diagnostic tap; an ascitic neutrophil count above 250/mm³ means SBP (BSG/BASL 2020). Treatment combines moderate salt restriction, diuretics, paracentesis with albumin and early antibiotics for infection.
keyMechanisms: Portal hypertension raises sinusoidal pressure and lymph formation.
Splanchnic vasodilatation lowers effective arterial volume and activates sodium retention.
Gut bacteria translocate to ascitic fluid with low protein and poor opsonic activity, causing SBP.
Infection and large fluid shifts can precipitate hepatorenal syndrome.

symptoms: Fever, abdominal pain, confusion or diarrhoea in SBP
redFlags: Fever, abdominal pain, encephalopathy or worsening kidney function: tap for SBP at once (BSG/BASL)
Gastrointestinal bleeding with ascites: needs antibiotic prophylaxis (BSG/BASL recommendation 2.7)
Sodium below 125 mmol/L or rising creatinine on diuretics
Tense ascites with breathlessness
precipitants: Alcohol, hepatitis B or C, MASLD

Secondary prophylaxis after SBP (BSG/BASL recommendation 2.8).

pathophysiology.summary: Deep vein thrombosis is clot in the deep veins, usually of the leg, arising from Virchow's triad: venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability. In India, common triggers include surgery, long immobilisation, trauma, pregnancy and the postpartum period, cancer, tuberculosis and dehydration. Proximal DVT can embolise to the lungs. Diagnosis combines the two-level Wells score with D-dimer and compression ultrasound (NICE NG158). Treatment is anticoagulation for at least 3 months, preferably with a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) such as apixaban or rivaroxaban; low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) is used in pregnancy, severe renal failure and some cancers.
keyMechanisms: Stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability (Virchow's triad) start thrombus in valve pockets.
Clot propagates proximally and obstructs venous return, causing swelling and pain.
Proximal clot can detach and cause pulmonary embolism.
Valve damage leads to post-thrombotic syndrome.

pathophysiology.summary: Pulmonary embolism is obstruction of the pulmonary arteries by thrombus, usually from leg or pelvic veins. Sudden rise in pulmonary vascular resistance strains the right ventricle; if it fails, cardiac output falls and shock follows. Risk ranges from small peripheral emboli to high-risk PE with haemodynamic instability, which carries high early mortality. Diagnosis follows a pre-test probability score, D-dimer when probability is low, and CTPA. Haemodynamically unstable patients need systemic thrombolysis; others are anticoagulated, preferably with a DOAC, for at least 3 months (ESC 2019; NICE NG158).
keyMechanisms: Thrombus from deep veins lodges in pulmonary arteries.
Raised pulmonary vascular resistance dilates and strains the right ventricle.
RV failure lowers LV filling and cardiac output, causing shock.
Ventilation-perfusion mismatch causes hypoxaemia.

physicalSigns: Hypotension, raised JVP in high-risk PE

RV dysfunction with raised troponin (intermediate-high risk)

pathophysiology.summary: Influenza is an acute viral respiratory infection with seasonal peaks in India, often during the monsoon and winter. Influenza A (H1N1) and other strains cause fever, cough and sore throat; most people recover, but pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and death occur, especially in high-risk groups: age 65 or more, pregnancy and up to 2 weeks postpartum, children under 5, chronic heart, lung, kidney, liver or neurological disease, diabetes, immunosuppression and severe obesity (MoHFW 2019). Viral replication and the host inflammatory response cause fever and airway damage.
Severe infection causes viral pneumonia and ARDS.
Damaged epithelium allows secondary bacterial pneumonia.

evidenceAudit.scope: Acute watery diarrhoea and dysentery in adults and adolescents in India: dehydration assessment, oral and IV rehydration, when to give antibiotics, amoebic dysentery and avoidance of fluoroquinolones, using NCDC-ICMR NTG 2025 section 4.2 and WHO rehydration plans. Childhood diarrhoea and cholera have separate topics.
findings: Antibiotics only with danger signs (azithromycin 500 mg once daily for 3 days first line; cefixime 400 mg twice daily or ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily for 5 days), stool microscopy in dysentery with metronidazole 400 mg three times daily for Entamoeba histolytica, and avoidance of fluoroquinolones because of high resistance in India checked against NCDC-ICMR NTG 2025 section 4.2.

Dehydration signs, Plan A ORS 300 mL per loose stool (over 20 kg), Plan B 75 mL/kg over 4 hours, Plan C Ringer lactate 100 mL/kg (30 mL/kg in 30 minutes then 70 mL/kg over 2.5 hours from 12 months of age), reassessment and fluid-overload signs checked against the WHO plans (MSF Appendix 14).
Not clinically reviewed.
unverifiedSections: The WHO plans in the opened source are written for children; Plan B volumes above 30 kg and Plan C timing for adults are extrapolated from the 12 months and older column.
NTG 2025 does not define 'danger signs' in the opened extract; usual signs (high fever, blood in stool, severe dehydration, sepsis, immunosuppression) are listed as practice.

pathophysiology.summary: Acute infectious diarrhoea in adults is usually viral or from toxin-producing bacteria and settles in a few days with fluids alone. The main danger is dehydration and electrolyte loss; dysentery (blood and mucus) suggests invasive bacteria such as Shigella or Campylobacter, or Entamoeba histolytica. Most adults do not need antibiotics; NTG 2025 reserves them for patients with danger signs and advises against fluoroquinolones because resistance is high in India. Oral rehydration solution (ORS) treats mild and moderate dehydration; severe dehydration needs rapid IV Ringer lactate.
keyMechanisms: Enterotoxins (for example from E. coli, Vibrio) drive chloride and water secretion: watery diarrhoea.
Invasive organisms damage the colonic mucosa: dysentery with blood and mucus.
Fluid loss causes hypovolaemia, acidosis and hypokalaemia.
Glucose-coupled sodium absorption remains intact, so ORS works.

pathophysiology.summary: Respiratory distress is one of the commonest reasons for newborn admission in India. In preterm babies the usual cause is respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) from surfactant deficiency, which collapses alveoli and causes grunting, retractions and hypoxaemia; in term babies, pneumonia or sepsis, transient tachypnoea and meconium aspiration are common. The ICMR workflow grades severity with the Silverman-Anderson score (SAS), gives oxygen to keep SpO2 between 91% and 95% (higher levels risk retinopathy of prematurity), starts continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) early, especially below 32 weeks, and refers for ventilation when distress is severe or CPAP fails.
keyMechanisms: Surfactant deficiency raises alveolar surface tension, so alveoli collapse at end-expiration (RDS).
Collapse reduces lung compliance and causes hypoxaemia and increased work of breathing.
Grunting is the baby's own PEEP against a partly closed glottis.
CPAP and surfactant keep alveoli open.

teaching.scope: Newborn respiratory distress in Indian units.
learningObjectives: Score distress with SAS.
Target SpO2 91–95%.
Start CPAP early and know when to refer.
keyPoints: Respiratory rate above 60, retractions, grunting or cyanosis = distress.
Oxygen 0.5–1 L/min by prongs; SpO2 91–95%.
Below 32 weeks: early CPAP.
SAS 5 or more or FiO2 above 60–70%: ventilate or refer.
pitfalls: Routine blood tests and X-rays in every baby.
Unnecessary IV fluids instead of feeds.
